chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yaqtin, from Al-Husayn ibn Mayyah, from his father, from Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him), who said:
Indeed, Iblees analogised himself with Adam (peace be upon him), so he said:
"You created me from fire and You created him from clay."
And had he compared the essence from which God created Adam (peace be upon him) with the fire, that would have been more light and radiance than the fire.

key_terms.الْجَوْهَرَ: jawhar: the primordial essence or substance from which Adam was created — here described as more luminous than fire, exposing Iblees's analogy as baseless
key_terms.ضِيَاءً: ḍiyāʾ: radiance, brilliance — paired with nūr to amplify the contrast between Adam's essence and fire
key_terms.قَاسَ: qāsa: he analogised/compared — the same verbal root as qiyās, the juristic method of analogical reasoning that this chapter of al-Kafi critiques
key_terms.نُوراً: nūr: light, luminosity — the spiritual quality in which Adam's essence surpasses Iblees's material

ai.seo_question: Why does Imam al-Sadiq (AS) in al-Kafi refute the analogy Iblees made between fire and clay?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) exposes the fatal flaw in Iblees's analogical reasoning (qiyas): Iblees compared his material of creation (fire) to Adam's (clay) and concluded his own superiority. The Imam overturns this by revealing that the primordial essence (jawhar) from which God fashioned Adam was in fact more luminous and radiant than fire itself — making Iblees's analogy not merely wrong but inverted. The placement in al-Kulayni's chapter on bid'a, ra'y, and analogies signals that this hadith is a theological proof-text against the use of qiyas in Islamic law.
